In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the activation region of PCPB contains a high percentage (approximately 30%) of acidic residues which, together with a low content of basic residues, are probably responsible for its proteolytic resistance.
the activation region of PCPB contains all the information necessary for trypsin to produce the activation of the zymogen in vitro and to generate the characteristic intermediates.

the porcine PCP A and PCPB precursors share the following common features: both are single-chain proteins; both are composed of an activation region of 95 residues and a CPB region of 250 residues; and both have an activation region which is rich in acidic residues and poor in methionines, cysteines, and other posttranslational modification sites, and which presents a low but statistically significant homology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the activation process of PCPB, trypsin first cleaves the activation region at a single site, then cleaves the released activation peptides at several sites, and finally releases the CPB region as a single entity, which is then processed by CPB itself.

, as in the case of other zymogens, activation of PCPB is a complex process which involves the proteolytic release of an activation region, a quick-trimming of its C-terminus, and the formation of the active enzyme.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the activation region of PCPB is an extremely poor substrate for trypsin, and that the activation process proceeds by a sequence of proteolytic events that is not compatible with a mechanism of autocatalytic activation.
the activation process of PCPB is more complex than that of PCPA, and that the activation region of PCPB has a sequence that is quite different from the corresponding one of PCPA.
, although procarboxypeptides B and A are very similar in structure, their activation mechanisms are quite different.
